title: The professional team REVIC put in place
body:
## The Playbook, Not the Checkbook

When REVIC secured 66.76% of Unitika's voting rights via a ¥20 billion Class C preferred share injection on April 30, 2025, the capital was only half the transaction. What the Regional Economic Vitalization Corporation of Japan deployed alongside the money was a carefully constructed operating team — assembled, as subsequent events would confirm, for a specific and time-limited mission. The April 2025 board reconstitution was not a governance reshuffle of the kind that follows a routine rights offering. It was a professional restructuring team placement: a career-engineer CEO paired with a REVIC Managing Director embedded as Vice President, backstopped by an outside director who had executed an almost identical turnaround at a different 130-year-old Osaka industrial company, and a senior partner from one of Osaka's major insolvency-practice law firms. One year later, REVIC's April 27, 2026 announcement — Kashiwagi Hisami pulled back to part-time, Furukawa Minoru retiring, the restructuring scaffolding beginning to come down — confirmed the deployment was always time-boxed. The question now is what it produced.

## The Engineer at the Helm

Fujii Minoru joined Unitika in 1987, fresh from Kyoto Institute of Technology's Graduate School of Textile Science with a master's degree in fiber science. He spent the next 38 years moving through the company's technical divisions, accumulating the kind of granular operational knowledge that general managers rarely have. He ran nylon fiber manufacturing in 2008, moved to plant director of the glass fiber operation in 2012, took over the glass fiber business division as a whole in 2019 — picking up an executive officer title in the same step — and was appointed head of the Technology Supervision Division in October 2023. On April 30, 2025, he became Representative Director, President and CEO.

Fujii is, by his own description, "the only career employee in management." The formulation carries weight. His entire leadership team at the time of his appointment included a REVIC-deployed operative, a former president of Hitachi Zosen, and a restructuring lawyer — none of whom had spent a day inside Unitika's production lines. Fujii's value to REVIC was precisely this: a CEO who could communicate continuity to a workforce absorbing the shock of the textile-exit announcement while providing the technical credibility that the specialty-materials pivot required. He was also, critically, in the room when the decision to withdraw from textiles was being debated. His elevation was not an elevation of someone new; it was a formalization of someone who had already decided.

## The Operative

Kashiwagi Hisami is the REVIC playbook made visible. Born in October 1977, she joined Daiwa Securities in 2000 before moving to REVIC's predecessor organization, the Corporate Revitalization Support Organization, in February 2010. From there, her career follows the pattern of a professional turnaround operative: deployed into Yamgiwa Corporation as Executive Officer for the Production Distribution Division in August 2011, then into Kabe no Ana Corporation as Director of the Management Division from October 2015. She became a Managing Director at REVIC proper in January 2018 and has held that rank since, taking on outside director roles at Chushigai Corporation (March 2019) and Iwai Corporation (September 2021) alongside her institutional responsibilities.

On April 30, 2025, she was embedded inside Unitika as Representative Director and Vice President, with explicit and formal responsibility for the Structural Reform Promotion Office. She also took direct oversight of the industrial fiber and non-woven business divisions — the very segments undergoing the most disruptive transformation. Her share ownership as of the February 2025 disclosure: zero. This is not incidental. A REVIC operative deployed to execute a restructuring mandate does not take equity exposure; she takes operational authority. The absence of skin in the game is a governance signal, not an oversight — it confirms the role was conceived as a deployment, not a principal position.

Eleven months later, on April 27, 2026, Unitika published the [announcement](https://www.unitika.co.jp/news/ir/post_304.html) that Kashiwagi would transition to a part-time, non-executive Director role effective June 26, 2026. The stated rationale: "business recovery plan progressing smoothly; structural reforms largely complete; enabling new management to focus on growth strategy." The language is careful and optimistic — perhaps deliberately so — but the cadence is unmistakable. A REVIC Managing Director was inserted into a portfolio company as its second-ranking executive, given a defined operational mandate, and extracted in roughly one year. This is how professional restructuring deployments work.

## The Precedent

Furukawa Minoru is on the Unitika board for one reason that has nothing to do with governance form. Born in June 1943, he graduated from Osaka University's Faculty of Economics in 1966 and joined Hitachi Zosen Corporation the same year. He rose through the company over four decades, spent time at the Singapore posting in 1976, and became Hitachi Zosen's 17th President in 2005, a position he held for eight years through 2013.

The eight years matter. When Furukawa took the helm of Hitachi Zosen, he inherited a company that had been a dominant name in Japanese heavy industry for 130 years and was then struggling under the weight of what that legacy had become. What he executed was a deliberate pivot away from shipbuilding toward environmental technology — filtration systems, waste-to-energy, water treatment — framing the transformation publicly as a "second founding" aimed at building a ¥1 trillion company by 2030 on the company's 130th anniversary. His recurring phrase, the "land-based Hitachi Zosen," became the shorthand for a thesis that industrial heritage need not be the ceiling of ambition.

The intellectual template is exact. Unitika is 137 years old. It is pivoting away from commodity textiles toward specialty materials. REVIC is the restructuring catalyst. And sitting on the board is the man who did the closest comparable thing at another Osaka industrial institution. Furukawa currently holds concurrent roles as Non-Executive Director at Ikeda Senshu Bank and senior positions at the Osaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Kansai Economic Federation — the connective tissue of Kansai industrial capital. He is retiring from the Unitika board on June 26, 2026. His contribution was the loan of a precedent at the moment when the board needed one most.

## The Lawyer Who Is Not Ceremonial

Horino Keiko graduated from Osaka University's Faculty of Law in March 2004, completed the 58th cohort of the Judicial Training Institute in October 2005, was admitted to the Osaka Bar the same month, and joined Kitahama Law Offices immediately. She made partner in January 2013, at what would have been roughly her seventh year of practice.

Kitahama is not a general commercial firm with a small restructuring desk. It is one of Osaka's established business law firms with a substantial insolvency practice, and Horino does this work professionally. Her documented practice areas span civil rehabilitation, corporate reorganization, and bankruptcy liquidation procedures alongside finance, M&A, real estate, and energy. She is a member of the National Insolvency Practice Network. She holds a Guest Professor appointment at Osaka University's Graduate School of Advanced Judicial Studies in trust law since 2021. She has concurrent outside director roles at Medical Ichiko Group (since 2021) and Orbis System Corporation (since 2023).

Her appointment to the Unitika board concurrent with REVIC's capital injection is a working appointment, not a ceremonial one. A company that has just received ¥43 billion in bank debt forgiveness from MUFG, Mizuho, and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust, while simultaneously negotiating the sale of multiple business divisions to buyers including Seiren, Shikibo, and Zuiko Corporation, needs a sitting outside director who can read a civil rehabilitation filing, not one who can speak generally about good governance. Horino continues on the post-June 2026 board — the one signal of continuity in an otherwise substantially reconstituted room.

Ishikawa Michiko, by contrast, presents a thinner profile. A practicing attorney at Yokohama Minami Law Office with a Kanagawa Bar Association registration from 2021 — a relatively recent vintage — her specific practice specialty is not publicly detailed to a level of precision. She does not appear on the post-June 2026 board list, replaced by the incoming Hakomori Kazuaki. Whether her exit reflects a rotating slot or a judgment about seniority is not stated, but the contrast with Horino's retention is suggestive.

## The Operating Bench

Below the restructuring team sits the trio that will actually run Unitika through the next phase. Misu Shuichi, 56, holds the CFO-equivalent position — finance, legal compliance, IT systems, and sustainability — the institutional plumbing without which restructuring commitments are aspirational. Kobayashi Eiji, 43, ran fiber and business planning through the restructuring year and inherits Strategic Planning, IR, and Functional Materials in June 2026, a portfolio that makes him the face of the company's external narrative. Fujimoto Shinji, 48, runs the operating core that REVIC is actually betting on: polymer films, glass fiber, anisotropic conductive film, glass beads. In June 2026, his responsibility envelope expands to include Reform Implementation — the work that Kashiwagi will no longer be executing on a full-time basis.

| Director | Age | Core Portfolio (June 2026) | Signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Misu Shuichi | 56 | Finance / Legal / IT / Sustainability | Institutional continuity |
| Kobayashi Eiji | 43 | Strategic Planning / IR / Functional Materials | Owns the external story |
| Fujimoto Shinji | 48 | Polymer / Glass Fiber / ACF / Reform Implementation | Owns the operating core |

One governance footnote that observers may note: the incoming Standing Auditor, Iwafuji Atsushi, holds a concurrent appointment as Executive Officer for Corporate Planning. An auditor who simultaneously sits in the executive structure audits, at least in part, decisions in which he has been a participant. This is an unusual structural arrangement and REVIC has offered no specific rationale for it.

Nakano Shinsuke, 40, makes the opposite transition — promoted from Standing Auditor to Director, Senior Executive Officer, taking HR and administration with secondary Finance and Reform responsibilities. The movement of an auditor into the executive function is unusual as a directional flow; it may reflect a practical judgment about Nakano's institutional knowledge of Unitika's compliance posture at a moment when the company is managing complex multi-party divestitures simultaneously.

## What the Team Produced

The April 2026 announcement closes a recognizable chapter. REVIC assembled a professional restructuring team in April 2025, embedded its own Managing Director at the vice-presidential level with explicit structural reform authority, placed a Hitachi Zosen turnaround veteran in the room to lend precedent and institutional gravity, retained a working insolvency lawyer as outside director, and gave the whole arrangement roughly twelve months to execute. The operating metrics through the first nine months of FY3/26 — cumulative revenue of ¥95.6 billion, operating profit of ¥9.0 billion representing a 110.3% year-on-year increase, and an equity ratio of 25.2% — suggest the restructuring scaffolding did its job. The nonwovens business found a buyer in Zuiko Corporation. Textile operations are being sold to Seiren and Shikibo. The PPS film joint development with DIC was announced at CES 2026.

What was not produced, at least not publicly, is a granular picture of what Misu, Kobayashi, and Fujimoto are inheriting as standalone management challenges. A 110% operating profit increase is a meaningful number, but it was generated by a team that included Kashiwagi running structural reform full-time and Furukawa's implicit endorsement of the second-founding thesis. Whether the three career-Unitika executives can sustain operating discipline in specialty films and glass fiber — businesses that require continuous customer-specific development, thin tolerances, and long sales cycles — without the restructuring scaffolding is what the next three to four years will actually test. REVIC's playbook had a beginning, a middle, and an explicit ending. The ending is June 2026. The judgment comes after.
